Chapter 9  ·  Machine Learning Foundations

Soft Margin SVMs
and Feature Engineering

From rigid hyperplanes to flexible, noise-tolerant classifiers that bend the rules — and the space itself.

Learning Objectives

  • Articulate why hard margin SVMs fail on non-separable or noisy data and identify the two core failure modes.
  • Derive the soft margin SVM primal optimization problem by introducing slack variables $\zeta_i \ge 0$.
  • Interpret the geometric meaning of a slack variable in terms of margin violation distance.
  • Explain the role of the regularization hyperparameter $C$ and its effect on the bias–variance tradeoff.
  • Identify support vectors in a soft margin setting, including properly classified, margin-violating, and misclassified points.
  • Construct a feature lifting map $\Phi$ that transforms a non-linear decision boundary into a linear one in a higher-dimensional space.
  • Prove that linear separability in $\Phi$-space is equivalent to separability by a hypersphere in the original space.
  • Enumerate the quadric decision boundaries achievable by appending all degree-2 monomials as features.
  • Analyze the computational trade-off between polynomial degree $p$ and lifted feature dimension $O(d^p)$.
  • Apply the complete soft margin SVM pipeline — with polynomial features — to a practical classification problem.

9.1 Motivation: Limitations of Hard Margin SVMs

The hard margin support vector machine, introduced in Chapter 8, is an elegant and powerful algorithm. By finding the maximum-width slab that separates two classes, it produces classifiers that are provably robust — wide margins correlate with good generalization. But real data is messy. Two distinct failure modes make the hard margin SVM impractical in many settings, and understanding them precisely is the first step toward the soft margin correction.

The first failure mode is fundamental: hard margin SVMs simply do not have a solution when the training data is not linearly separable. The optimization problem requires that every positive training point satisfies $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha \ge 1$ and every negative point satisfies $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha \le -1$. If no hyperplane can simultaneously satisfy all these constraints, the feasible region of the optimization problem is empty. The solver returns nothing useful.

The second failure mode is subtler but equally damaging: even when the data is linearly separable, the hard margin machine can be extremely sensitive to individual training points. Adding or removing a single point can dramatically shift the decision boundary — a property we call outlier sensitivity. In most practical settings, training data contains measurement errors, labeling mistakes, or simply points that are statistically unusual. Placing enormous weight on such a point may produce a classifier that performs well on the training set but poorly on unseen data.

9.1.1 Linear Non-Separability

Formally, two labeled sets $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $y_i \in \{-1, +1\}$ are linearly separable if there exists a vector $\mathbf{w}$ and scalar $\alpha$ such that $y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha) \ge 1$ for all $i$. When this condition fails, no feasible solution exists for the hard margin primal, and any standard quadratic program solver will report infeasibility. In practice, real-world classification tasks — spam detection, image recognition, medical diagnosis — almost always involve classes whose Bayes-optimal boundary is non-linear, making linear non-separability the rule rather than the exception.

Definition · Linear Separability

A labeled dataset $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ is linearly separable if there exist $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d \setminus \{\mathbf{0}\}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $$y_i\bigl(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha\bigr) \ge 1 \quad \forall\, i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}.$$ If no such $(\mathbf{w}, \alpha)$ exists, the dataset is linearly non-separable and the hard margin SVM primal has an empty feasible region.

9.1.2 Outlier Sensitivity

Even when the data is linearly separable, the hard margin SVM is determined entirely by the support vectors — the handful of points that lie exactly on the margin boundaries. Any point far from the boundary has zero influence on the solution. But a single poorly-placed training example can become a support vector and completely alter the decision boundary. Figure 9.1 illustrates this phenomenon: one additional training point on the right causes the boundary to rotate from a diagonal line to a nearly horizontal one.

Figure 9.1. Outlier sensitivity of the hard margin SVM. Both panels show the same underlying class structure; the right panel adds a single red-star outlier. The decision boundary (dark line) and margin slab (gold fill) rotate substantially in response to this one extra point, despite its statistical unrepresentativeness. Blue circles are class $+1$; green crosses are class $-1$.
Intuition · Why Outliers Matter So Much

The hard margin SVM "listens" only to the points closest to the boundary — the support vectors. Every other training point is irrelevant to the solution. This is actually one of the SVM's great strengths in clean data: it ignores uninformative interior points. But the same property is a weakness when an outlier accidentally ends up near the boundary. The algorithm has no mechanism to say "this point seems unusual; I should trust it less." It treats all training points as equally reliable. The soft margin is the fix: it introduces a knob that controls how much any single point can perturb the boundary.

💡
Key insight: Both failure modes — non-separability and outlier sensitivity — stem from the same underlying cause: the hard margin's demand that every training point be correctly classified with a full-unit margin. The soft margin relaxes exactly this demand.

9.2 Slack Variables and the Soft Margin Formulation

The soft margin SVM addresses both failure modes by allowing training points to violate the margin — but at a cost. The mathematical device that operationalizes this idea is the slack variable. Rather than demanding that each training point satisfy its margin constraint exactly, we introduce a non-negative variable $\zeta_i$ for each training point that measures how much that point is "allowed" to cheat. Setting $\zeta_i = 0$ recovers the hard margin constraint for point $i$; setting $\zeta_i > 0$ gives point $i$ some slack to intrude into or cross the slab.

The elegance of this approach is that it converts an infeasible optimization problem into a feasible one: with enough slack, any hyperplane can be made to "satisfy" the constraints for any dataset. The challenge, then, is not feasibility but rather controlling the total amount of slack used — which is precisely what the objective function will penalize.

9.2.1 Introducing Slack Variables

Definition · Soft Margin Constraints

Given training data $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $y_i \in \{-1,+1\}$, the soft margin constraints with slack variables $\boldsymbol{\zeta} = (\zeta_1, \ldots, \zeta_n)$ are: $$y_i\bigl(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha\bigr) \ge 1 - \zeta_i \quad \forall\, i, \label{eq:soft-constraint}$$ $$\zeta_i \ge 0 \quad \forall\, i. \label{eq:slack-nonneg}$$ When $\zeta_i = 0$, point $i$ satisfies the hard margin constraint exactly. When $0 < \zeta_i \le 1$, point $i$ lies inside the margin slab but is still correctly classified. When $\zeta_i > 1$, point $i$ is misclassified.

Comparing with the hard margin constraint $y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha) \ge 1$, the modification is minimal: we subtract $\zeta_i$ from the right-hand side. When $\zeta_i = 0$ the constraints are identical; every unit of slack "buys" a relaxation of exactly that amount. Note that we require $\zeta_i \ge 0$ — we never allow slack to make a constraint easier than the hard version would be for points that are already correctly classified with margin. Points that naturally satisfy the margin constraint are assigned $\zeta_i = 0$ automatically by any reasonable objective (since making $\zeta_i$ larger would only increase the penalty term in the objective).

9.2.2 Geometric Interpretation of Slack

The slack variable $\zeta_i$ has a precise geometric meaning. Recall that the signed distance from training point $\mathbf{x}_i$ to the decision boundary $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha = 0$ is $y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha) / \|\mathbf{w}\|$. The margin boundary on the positive side is at signed distance $1/\|\mathbf{w}\|$ from the decision boundary. The slack variable $\zeta_i$ measures, in units of $\|\mathbf{w}\|$, how far point $i$ has penetrated beyond its margin boundary. Concretely, the distance from $\mathbf{x}_i$ to the margin boundary it should be beyond is $\zeta_i / \|\mathbf{w}\|$.

Example · Reading Slack from a Diagram

Setup. Suppose the optimal solution has $\|\mathbf{w}\| = 2$, and the margin width is $1/\|\mathbf{w}\| = 0.5$. Consider three training points: (A) correctly classified, 0.8 units from boundary — $\zeta_A = 0$ since $y_A(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_A + \alpha) = 1.6 \ge 1$. (B) inside the slab, 0.3 units from boundary — $y_B(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_B + \alpha) = 0.6$, so $\zeta_B = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4$. (C) misclassified, 0.4 units on the wrong side — $y_C(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_C + \alpha) = -0.8$, so $\zeta_C = 1 - (-0.8) = 1.8$.

Takeaway. Point A incurs zero penalty. Point B, inside the slab, has $0 < \zeta_B < 1$. Point C, wrongly classified, has $\zeta_C > 1$. Notice that $\zeta_C / \|\mathbf{w}\| = 1.8/2 = 0.9$ is the physical distance from point C to the margin boundary — a direct measure of how badly it was misclassified.

Figure 9.2. Geometric interpretation of slack variables. The gold-shaded band is the margin slab; the navy line is the decision boundary. Blue circles are class $+1$; green crosses are class $-1$. Points labeled (1) and (2) lie inside the slab and have $0 < \zeta_i \le 1$ — the red arrows show the distance $\zeta_i/\|\mathbf{w}\|$ each point must travel to reach its margin boundary. Point (3) is on the wrong side of the decision boundary, so $\zeta_3 > 1$. The arrow length equals $\zeta_i/\|\mathbf{w}\|$, the physical margin violation.

9.2.3 Support Vectors Revisited

With slack, the definition of "support vector" becomes richer. In the hard margin setting, support vectors are precisely the points on the margin boundary. In the soft margin setting, we identify support vectors as the points that actively influence the decision boundary, which includes a broader class.

Definition · Support Vectors (Soft Margin)

In a soft margin SVM solution $(\mathbf{w}^*, \alpha^*, \boldsymbol{\zeta}^*)$, the support vectors are all training points $\mathbf{x}_i$ satisfying at least one of:

  • $\zeta_i^* > 0$ — the point violates the margin (lies inside the slab or is misclassified), OR
  • $y_i(\mathbf{w}^* \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha^*) = 1$ — the point lies exactly on the margin boundary (with $\zeta_i^* = 0$).
Points satisfying $y_i(\mathbf{w}^* \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha^*) > 1$ with $\zeta_i^* = 0$ are non-support vectors and do not influence the solution. Removing them would not change $\mathbf{w}^*$ or $\alpha^*$.

Warning · Redefining "Margin"

In the hard margin setting, the margin was defined as the distance from the decision boundary to the nearest training point. This definition breaks down when points are allowed to violate the slab. The correct definition for soft margin (and indeed for hard margin, stated more fundamentally) is: $$\text{Margin} = \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}$$ where $\mathbf{w}$ is the weight vector returned by the optimization. This quantity is determined by the optimization objective $\min \|\mathbf{w}\|^2$ and does not depend on where the training points actually land relative to the slab. Do not confuse $1/\|\mathbf{w}\|$ with the distance to the nearest point — in the soft margin setting, those two quantities can differ substantially.

9.3 The Soft Margin Optimization Problem

We now have all the ingredients to write down the complete soft margin SVM. The objective must balance two competing desires: making the margin $1/\|\mathbf{w}\|$ as wide as possible (equivalently, minimizing $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$), and keeping the total margin violation $\sum_i \zeta_i$ as small as possible. These two goals can conflict — widening the margin may force some points into the slab, increasing slack. The hyperparameter $C$ controls the trade-off.

9.3.1 Primal Formulation

Soft Margin SVM Primal
$$\min_{\mathbf{w},\,\alpha,\,\boldsymbol{\zeta}} \;\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^n \zeta_i$$ $$\text{subject to} \quad y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha) \ge 1 - \zeta_i, \quad \zeta_i \ge 0, \quad \forall\, i.$$

The decision variables are $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, and $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \in \mathbb{R}^n_{\ge 0}$. The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in front of $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$ is a convention that simplifies the dual derivation (see Section 10.1) without affecting the solution. The constant $C > 0$ is the regularization hyperparameter: it specifies, in the same units as the problem, how expensive each unit of slack is relative to narrowing the margin.

Example · Verifying the Soft Margin Optimality Conditions

Setup. Consider a one-dimensional problem ($d = 1$) with two training points: $x_1 = 1, y_1 = +1$ and $x_2 = -1, y_2 = -1$. These are linearly separable, so with large enough $C$ we expect $\zeta_1 = \zeta_2 = 0$ and recovery of the hard margin solution.

Hard margin solution. The decision boundary is $w \cdot x + \alpha = 0$. By symmetry, $\alpha = 0$. The margin constraints give $w \ge 1$ and $-(-w) \ge 1 \Rightarrow w \ge 1$. Minimizing $w^2/2$ gives $w^* = 1$, margin $= 1/|w^*| = 1$.

Small-C regime. Let $C = 0.1$. Now it may be cheaper to allow some slack than to maintain $w = 1$. Setting $w = 0.5$: the constraint for $x_1$ becomes $0.5 \ge 1 - \zeta_1$, so $\zeta_1 \ge 0.5$; similarly $\zeta_2 \ge 0.5$. The objective is $\frac{1}{2}(0.25) + 0.1(1.0) = 0.225$. With $w = 1$ and zero slack, objective $= 0.5$. So with tiny $C$, the algorithm prefers a narrower margin with slack to a wide margin without it — exactly the underfitting regime described in Section 9.4.

Result. For $C \ge 0.5$, the zero-slack solution is optimal; for $C < 0.5$, the soft solution wins. This shows that the crossover between regimes is determined by the problem geometry and $C$ jointly.

9.3.2 Quadratic Program Structure

The soft margin SVM is a quadratic program (QP): an optimization problem with a convex quadratic objective and linear constraints. Quadratic programs are extremely well-studied and have efficient solvers.

Definition · Quadratic Program

A quadratic program (QP) is an optimization problem of the form $$\min_{\mathbf{z}} \;\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{z}^\top Q \mathbf{z} + \mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{z} \quad \text{subject to} \quad A\mathbf{z} \le \mathbf{b},$$ where $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$ is positive semi-definite, $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times m}$, and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^k$. When $Q$ is positive definite, the objective is strictly convex and the problem has a unique global minimum.

The soft margin primal lives in $d + n + 1$ dimensions: $d$ dimensions for $\mathbf{w}$, $n$ for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$, and $1$ for the bias $\alpha$. It has $2n$ constraints: $n$ margin constraints and $n$ non-negativity constraints on the slacks. When $d \ll n$ (many training points, few features), the dual formulation (which operates in $n$ dimensions, as we will see in Chapter 10) can be more efficient. When $d \gg n$ (many features, few points), the primal is preferred.

Data Science Application · The Hinge Loss Connection

The soft margin objective can be rewritten in a form that illuminates its connection to regularized empirical risk minimization. Note that for any fixed $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$, the optimal slack for point $i$ is $\zeta_i^* = \max(0,\, 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha))$. Substituting this back into the objective: $$\min_{\mathbf{w},\alpha} \;\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^n \max\bigl(0,\, 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha)\bigr).$$ The function $\ell_{\text{hinge}}(z) = \max(0, 1-z)$ is the hinge loss, one of the most important loss functions in machine learning. The soft margin SVM is therefore equivalent to $\ell_2$-regularized empirical risk minimization with the hinge loss — a fact that connects SVMs to logistic regression, neural network training, and modern deep learning frameworks where regularization + empirical loss is the standard paradigm.

9.4 The Regularization Hyperparameter C

The parameter $C$ is not learned from data — it must be specified before running the optimization. This makes it a hyperparameter, and choosing it correctly is critical to getting good performance. The word "regularization" in its name is deliberate: small $C$ imposes stronger regularization (a bias toward wider margins and simpler boundaries), while large $C$ reduces regularization (forcing the boundary to accommodate the training data more precisely).

Understanding the dual role of $C$ — as a balance between margin width and slack penalty, and as a knob controlling the bias-variance tradeoff — is essential for applying soft margin SVMs in practice. We examine this relationship from four distinct angles: the objective function interpretation, the over/underfitting perspective, outlier robustness, and boundary complexity.

9.4.1 Small vs. Large C: A Four-Way Comparison

Figure 9.3. Effect of the hyperparameter $C$ on the decision boundary and margin slab (gold region). The same training set is shown in all four panels; only $C$ changes. At $C = 0.01$ (far left) the margin is very wide and many points are allowed to violate it. At $C = 50$ (far right) the margin has narrowed drastically and the algorithm tries to push every point outside the slab. Blue circles: class $+1$; green crosses: class $-1$.
AspectSmall CLarge C
Primary goalMaximize margin width $1/\|\mathbf{w}\|$Minimize total slack $\sum_i \zeta_i$
Behavior limit$C \to 0$: boundary becomes uninformative$C \to \infty$: approaches hard margin SVM
Fitting regimeUnderfitting (training accuracy can suffer)Overfitting (training accuracy near perfect)
Outlier sensitivityLow — allows outliers to be slack-absorbedHigh — forces boundary to accommodate outliers
Boundary shapeSimple, flat (few support vectors active)Complex, sinuous (many support vectors)
Running timeFaster (relaxed feasibility)Slower (approaches infeasible hard margin)
Intuition · C as a Budget for Margin Violation

Think of $C$ as the price of slack: each unit of $\zeta_i$ costs $C$ dollars. The algorithm has a fixed "moral budget" — it wants to minimize the total cost $\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C \sum_i \zeta_i$. When $C$ is large, slack is expensive, so the algorithm is frugal — it refuses to let points violate the margin and instead tightens $\mathbf{w}$ to push them out. When $C$ is small, slack is cheap, so the algorithm is happy to let many points penetrate the slab and focuses instead on widening the margin. This "economy of slack" metaphor makes the $C$ tradeoff intuitive.

9.4.2 Validation and the U-shaped Error Curve

Because no closed-form formula gives the optimal $C$, we rely on cross-validation. We train the SVM for a grid of $C$ values (typically logarithmically spaced, e.g., $C \in \{10^{-3}, 10^{-2}, \ldots, 10^3\}$) and evaluate validation error for each. The result is a characteristic U-shaped curve: error is high for very small $C$ (underfitting), decreases to a minimum at the sweet spot, and rises again for very large $C$ (overfitting).

Figure 9.4. Training error (blue, solid) and validation error (red, dashed) as a function of the regularization hyperparameter $C$ on a log scale. Training error decreases monotonically as $C$ increases — larger $C$ forces the algorithm to fit the training data more tightly. Validation error exhibits the characteristic U-shape: too small $C$ gives underfitting; too large gives overfitting. The gold dotted line marks the optimal $C$ that minimizes validation error. In practice, this curve is estimated empirically via $k$-fold cross-validation.
Warning · C Interacts with Feature Scaling

The regularization hyperparameter $C$ is sensitive to the scale of the input features $\mathbf{x}_i$. If you multiply all feature values by a constant $s$, the geometry of the problem changes: $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$ changes relative to the slack terms, shifting the effective regularization. Always standardize or normalize features (e.g., z-score each feature to mean 0, variance 1) before running an SVM, and retune $C$ after any change in preprocessing. Failing to do so can make a well-tuned $C$ completely ineffective.

📌
In practice: Start with a coarse logarithmic grid search over $C \in \{10^{-3}, 10^{-1}, 10, 10^3\}$, then refine around the best value. Always use $k$-fold cross-validation (typically $k = 5$ or $k = 10$) rather than a single held-out validation set to reduce variance in the estimate.

9.5 Feature Engineering and Lifting Maps

Soft margin SVMs can tolerate noisy, imperfect data — but they remain linear classifiers. Their decision boundaries are still hyperplanes, and no amount of tuning $C$ will help when the true decision boundary is fundamentally non-linear. A different strategy is needed: rather than changing the algorithm, we change the representation of the data.

The key idea is feature engineering via lifting: we define a map $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D$ (with $D > d$) that transforms each training point into a higher-dimensional representation. We then apply a linear classifier to the lifted points $\Phi(\mathbf{x}_i)$. If $\Phi$ is chosen wisely, the classes that were non-linearly separable in $\mathbb{R}^d$ become linearly separable in $\mathbb{R}^D$. The linear boundary in $\mathbb{R}^D$ "folds back down" into a non-linear boundary in the original space $\mathbb{R}^d$.

This approach is remarkably general: it works with any linear classifier — SVMs, perceptrons, logistic regression — and any non-linear target boundary, as long as $\Phi$ captures the right structure. The challenge lies in choosing $\Phi$ appropriately for the problem at hand.

9.5.1 The Idea of Lifting

Definition · Feature Lifting Map

A feature lifting map (or feature map) is a function $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D$ with $D \ge d$ that embeds the original feature space into a higher-dimensional space. Training is performed on the lifted dataset $\{(\Phi(\mathbf{x}_i), y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$. A linear classifier applied in $\mathbb{R}^D$ induces a (generally non-linear) decision boundary in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The decision function is $$f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}) + \alpha,$$ and the decision boundary $\{f(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}$ is a non-linear surface in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for non-linear $\Phi$.

9.5.2 Circular and Spherical Decision Boundaries

As a concrete and important first example, consider the goal of classifying points that are arranged in concentric rings — an inner class and an outer class. No hyperplane can separate these, but a circle or sphere can. Can we design a lifting map that converts this circle-separability problem into a linear-separability problem?

The answer is yes, and the required map is elegant: we add a single new feature equal to the squared Euclidean norm of $\mathbf{x}$.

Definition · Parabolic Lifting Map

The parabolic lifting map $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ is defined by $$\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{x} \\ \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_d \\ x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_d^2 \end{pmatrix}.$$ This map embeds $\mathbb{R}^d$ onto the paraboloid $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_d, x_{d+1}) : x_{d+1} = \|\mathbf{x}\|^2\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$.

The geometric picture is striking: points near the origin get lifted to low heights on the paraboloid, while points far from the origin get lifted to high heights. An inner ring and an outer ring, which overlap in projection onto $\mathbb{R}^d$, are now well-separated in height along the $(d+1)$-th coordinate. A horizontal hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ — defined by $x_{d+1} = c$ for some constant $c$ — cuts the paraboloid at exactly the points where $\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 = c$, which is a $(d-1)$-sphere of radius $\sqrt{c}$ in the original space.

Figure 9.5. The parabolic lifting map in action. Left: original 2D space — blue circles (class $+1$) form an inner cluster; green crosses (class $-1$) form an outer ring; no hyperplane separates them, but a dashed red circle does. Center: the lifted 3D space — points lie on a paraboloid where height $= x_1^2 + x_2^2$; the gold semi-transparent plane separates the two classes linearly. Right: projecting the plane's intersection with the paraboloid back to 2D recovers the circular decision boundary (red solid line), matching the true boundary exactly.

9.5.3 The Parabolic Lifting Theorem

Theorem · Parabolic Lifting and Hyperspherical Separability

Let $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ be the parabolic lifting map. A dataset $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}$ is linearly separable in $\Phi$-space if and only if it is separable by a hypersphere (possibly of infinite radius, i.e., a hyperplane) in the original space $\mathbb{R}^d$.

Proof

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose the lifted points $\{\Phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\}$ are linearly separable with hyperplane $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{z} = \beta$, where $\mathbf{v} = (v_1, \ldots, v_d, v_{d+1})^\top$. A point $\mathbf{z} = \Phi(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x}, \|\mathbf{x}\|^2)$ is on the positive side when $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}) > \beta \;\iff\; \sum_{j=1}^d v_j x_j + v_{d+1}\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 > \beta.$$ If $v_{d+1} \neq 0$, divide through by $v_{d+1}$ and complete the square: $$\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 + \sum_{j=1}^d \frac{v_j}{v_{d+1}} x_j > \frac{\beta}{v_{d+1}} \;\iff\; \left\|\mathbf{x} + \frac{\mathbf{v}_{1:d}}{2v_{d+1}}\right\|^2 > \frac{\beta}{v_{d+1}} + \left\|\frac{\mathbf{v}_{1:d}}{2v_{d+1}}\right\|^2.$$ This is the interior/exterior of a hypersphere with center $\mathbf{c} = -\mathbf{v}_{1:d}/(2v_{d+1})$ and radius $\rho = \sqrt{\beta/v_{d+1} + \|\mathbf{c}\|^2}$. If $v_{d+1} = 0$, the inequality reduces to $\sum_j v_j x_j > \beta$, which is a hyperplane — a sphere of infinite radius.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose the original data is separated by the hypersphere $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}\|^2 = \rho^2$ (interior vs. exterior). Expanding: $$\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 - 2\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \|\mathbf{c}\|^2 \lessgtr \rho^2.$$ Rewrite using $\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x}, \|\mathbf{x}\|^2)$: $$\begin{pmatrix} -2\mathbf{c} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}) \lessgtr \rho^2 - \|\mathbf{c}\|^2.$$ This is a linear inequality in $\Phi(\mathbf{x})$. Since the spherical boundary separates the classes in $\mathbb{R}^d$, this linear inequality separates the lifted points in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$. The two implications together give the equivalence. □

Intuition · What the Proof is Really Saying

The proof is essentially a change of coordinates. The equation of a sphere in $\mathbb{R}^d$ involves $\|\mathbf{x}\|^2$ — a non-linear term. The lifting map $\Phi$ promotes this non-linear term to a new linear coordinate. Once promoted, the sphere equation becomes a linear equation in the new coordinates. A hyperplane in the lifted space is precisely the right geometric object to separate classes that are spherically separable in the original space. The magic is that a single extra dimension is sufficient, regardless of how large $d$ is.

9.6 Quadric Decision Boundaries

The parabolic map adds one feature and buys us spherical boundaries. But what if the true boundary is an ellipse, a hyperbola, or a more exotic quadric surface? To handle these, we need to enrich the lifting map further by including all degree-2 polynomial terms — the complete set of squares and cross-products of the original features.

The resulting class of decision boundaries, called quadrics, is rich enough to represent a wide variety of separating surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$, including spheres, ellipsoids, hyperboloids, paraboloids, cylinders, cones, hyperplanes, and their intersections. As we will see, this flexibility comes at a computational cost that grows quadratically with dimension.

9.6.1 All Degree-2 Monomials as Features

Definition · Degree-2 Lifting Map

The degree-2 lifting map $\Phi_2: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D$ (with $D = (d^2 + 3d)/2$) appends all degree-2 and degree-1 monomials: $$\Phi_2(\mathbf{x}) = \bigl(x_1^2,\, x_2^2,\, \ldots,\, x_d^2,\; x_1 x_2,\, x_1 x_3,\, \ldots,\, x_{d-1}x_d,\; x_1,\, x_2,\, \ldots,\, x_d\bigr)^\top.$$ When using a support vector machine (which handles the bias term $\alpha$ separately), no constant term $1$ is needed. For perceptrons or logistic regression, a constant $1$ must be appended explicitly.

The dimension of the lifted space is $d$ squares $+ \binom{d}{2}$ cross-terms $+ d$ linear terms $= d + d(d-1)/2 + d = (d^2 + 3d)/2$. For $d = 2$: $(4 + 6)/2 = 5$ dimensions. For $d = 10$: $(100 + 30)/2 = 65$ dimensions. For $d = 100$: $(10000 + 300)/2 = 5150$ dimensions. The quadratic blowup begins to be costly only around $d \approx 300$, which covers many practical settings comfortably.

Example · Degree-2 Lifting in 2D

For $d = 2$, the lifting map is $\Phi_2(x_1, x_2) = (x_1^2, x_2^2, x_1 x_2, x_1, x_2)^\top$. Running an SVM on the lifted points returns a weight vector $\mathbf{w} = (A, B, D, E, F)^\top$ and bias $\alpha = G$. The decision function in the original space is: $$f(x_1, x_2) = A x_1^2 + B x_2^2 + D x_1 x_2 + E x_1 + F x_2 + G = 0.$$ This is the general equation of a conic section in 2D. By choosing different values of $(A,B,D,E,F,G)$, the SVM can produce any circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola, pair of lines, or single line as its decision boundary — whatever best separates the training data.

9.6.2 A Taxonomy of Quadrics

Figure 9.6. A taxonomy of quadric decision boundaries achievable by the degree-2 lifting map in 2D. All are isosurfaces of the general quadratic $Ax_1^2 + Bx_2^2 + Dx_1x_2 + Ex_1 + Fx_2 + G = 0$. Top row (left to right): circle, ellipse, hyperbola. Bottom row: parabola, two parallel hyperplanes, degenerate (single hyperplane). This last case corresponds to all quadratic and cross-product coefficients being zero, recovering the hard margin SVM's linear boundary.

The degree-2 lifting map can produce all of the surfaces shown in Figure 9.6, plus high-dimensional generalizations: ellipsoids, hyperboloids, paraboloids, cylinders, and more. A key insight is that hyperplanes are a special case of quadrics: when all squared and cross-product coefficients in $\mathbf{w}$ are zero, the decision function reduces to a linear function, and the degree-2 SVM is equivalent to a standard linear SVM. Adding quadratic features can only improve or maintain performance — the linear case is still reachable.

Data Science Application · Quadratic Features in Practice

In machine learning pipelines, degree-2 feature maps are often implemented via sklearn.preprocessing.PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False). This is a standard preprocessing step before any linear classifier. The resulting model can capture interactions between features (via the cross-terms $x_i x_j$) as well as saturation effects (via the squared terms $x_i^2$). In genomics, for example, adding pairwise interaction terms between gene expression features allows linear models to detect epistatic interactions — gene pairs whose joint effect on a phenotype differs from the sum of individual effects. The degree-2 lifting is thus a principled way to move from "additive models" to "interactive models" at minimal algorithmic cost.

9.7 General Polynomial Features

The degree-2 lifting map can be generalized to arbitrary polynomial degree $p$. The degree-$p$ lifting map includes all monomials $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \cdots x_d^{a_d}$ with $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_d \le p$. This map can induce decision boundaries that are degree-$p$ algebraic hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$, capturing extremely complex geometric shapes.

Two important phenomena occur as we increase $p$: the lifted data becomes easier to separate (more dimensions means more room to find a separating hyperplane), and the margin in the lifted space can be wider, potentially leading to better generalization. However, the dimension of the lifted space grows as $O(d^p)$, eventually making direct computation infeasible for large $d$ or $p$. (The kernel trick, introduced in Chapter 10, resolves this computational problem elegantly.)

9.7.1 Degree-p Lifting

Definition · Degree-p Monomial Feature Map

The degree-$p$ feature map $\Phi_p: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{D_p}$ includes all monomials of degree at most $p$ (excluding the constant term when using an SVM): $$\Phi_p(\mathbf{x}) = \bigl(x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \cdots x_d^{a_d} : 1 \le a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_d \le p,\; a_j \ge 0\bigr)^\top.$$ The lifted dimension is $$D_p = \binom{d + p}{p} - 1 = \frac{(d+p)!}{d!\, p!} - 1.$$ For fixed $d$, this grows as $O(d^p / p!)$ as $p$ increases; for fixed $p$, it grows as $O(d^p)$ as $d$ increases.

Example · Dimension Blowup for Degree-3 in 2D

For $d = 2, p = 3$: $\binom{5}{3} - 1 = 9$ features. These are $x_1^3, x_2^3, x_1^2 x_2, x_1 x_2^2$ (cubic monomials), $x_1^2, x_2^2, x_1 x_2$ (quadratic monomials), and $x_1, x_2$ (linear). For $d = 10, p = 3$: $\binom{13}{3} - 1 = 285$ features. For $d = 100, p = 3$: $\binom{103}{3} - 1 = 176850$ features — already substantial. For $d = 100, p = 5$: $\binom{105}{5} - 1 \approx 9.6 \times 10^9$ — completely infeasible to store or compute directly.

9.7.2 Computational Cost and the Curse of Dimensionality

Figure 9.8. Lifted feature dimension $D_p$ as a function of original dimension $d$ for polynomial degrees 1, 2, and 3, shown on a log scale. The gold shading between degree-1 and degree-2 curves shows the "cost" of quadratic features; the red shading above shows the additional cost of degree-3 features. For $d > 30$, degree-3 lifting already produces tens of thousands of features, making direct computation prohibitive without the kernel trick.
Figure 9.7. Decision boundaries (navy contour) found by a linear SVM applied to degree-1, 2, and 5 polynomial feature maps on concentrically-arranged data. Left (degree 1): the linear boundary completely fails to separate the classes. Center (degree 2): the quadratic features allow a circular boundary — both classes are now well-separated. Right (degree 5): the degree-5 features allow an even more flexible boundary that can widen the margin further in some regions. Blue circles: class $+1$; green crosses: class $-1$. Background shading indicates the predicted class regions.
Theorem · Separability in High-Degree Polynomial Space

For any finite labeled dataset $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and all $\mathbf{x}_i$ distinct, there exists a polynomial degree $p^*$ such that the degree-$p^*$ lifted dataset is linearly separable.

Proof Sketch

By the Stone-Weierstrass theorem, polynomials are dense in the space of continuous functions on any compact set. More directly: for $n$ distinct points, we can construct an interpolating polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ that equals $+1$ on all positive points and $-1$ on all negative points. This polynomial, when added as a feature, gives a lifted space in which the signed label is a linear function of the features. A formal proof requires care about the interaction between the lifted feature representation and the linear separability condition, but the essence is that enough polynomial features can always interpolate the labels. □

Warning · High Degree Implies Overfitting

The preceding theorem is mathematically interesting but practically dangerous. Lifting to degree $p^* \approx n$ to guarantee linear separability means finding a polynomial that perfectly interpolates the training labels — the classic definition of overfitting. Every algorithm we study faces this tension: more expressive models memorize the training set but generalize poorly. The correct strategy is to choose the degree $p$ by validation (the same U-shaped curve as for $C$), not to blindly increase $p$ until separability is achieved. In most practical settings, degrees 2–4 with appropriate $C$ outperform very high degrees.

Data Science Application · Polynomial Features Beyond SVMs

Polynomial feature maps are not restricted to SVMs — they work with any linear model. In linear regression, adding polynomial features (via PolynomialFeatures followed by LinearRegression) gives polynomial regression. In logistic regression, they give logistic polynomial classifiers. In both cases, the algorithm remains mathematically linear — it optimizes a linear function of the lifted features — while the induced model in the original space is non-linear. This separation between the "learning algorithm" (which is always linear) and the "representation" (which can be highly non-linear) is a unifying theme of kernel methods, which we develop fully in Chapter 10.

💡
Looking ahead: The fundamental limitation of explicit polynomial lifting — the $O(d^p)$ dimension blowup — is resolved by the kernel trick (Chapter 10). The kernel trick allows the SVM to implicitly compute inner products in the degree-$p$ lifted space in $O(d)$ time, without ever constructing the $D_p$-dimensional feature vectors. This makes polynomial SVMs practical even for very large $d$ and $p$.

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter extended the hard margin SVM in two complementary directions. First, the soft margin formulation introduced slack variables $\zeta_i \ge 0$ to handle non-separable and noisy data, with the hyperparameter $C$ balancing margin width against total violation. Second, feature engineering via polynomial lifting maps transformed non-linear classification problems into linear ones in a higher-dimensional space, making SVMs applicable to a vastly wider class of decision boundaries including circles, ellipses, hyperboloids, and general degree-$p$ polynomial surfaces. Together, these two extensions — soft margins for robustness, feature lifting for expressiveness — bring the SVM from a mathematical curiosity into a practical and versatile machine learning tool.

SLACK VARIABLES

For each training point $i$, the slack $\zeta_i \ge 0$ measures how much the margin constraint is violated. $\zeta_i = 0$: no violation; $0 < \zeta_i \le 1$: inside the slab but correctly classified; $\zeta_i > 1$: misclassified. The physical violation distance is $\zeta_i / \|\mathbf{w}\|$.

SOFT MARGIN PRIMAL

Minimize $\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_i \zeta_i$ subject to $y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha) \ge 1 - \zeta_i$ and $\zeta_i \ge 0$. Variables: $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \in \mathbb{R}^n_{\ge 0}$. This is a QP in $d + n + 1$ dimensions with $2n$ constraints.

REGULARIZATION HYPERPARAMETER C

$C$ trades off margin width against slack. Small $C$: wide margin, underfitting risk, outlier-robust. Large $C$: narrow margin, overfitting risk, approximates hard margin. Chosen by cross-validation on a log-scale grid. Sensitive to feature scaling — always standardize first.

SUPPORT VECTORS (SOFT MARGIN)

All points with $\zeta_i > 0$ (margin violators) or $y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha) = 1$ (margin boundary points, $\zeta_i = 0$) are support vectors. Only support vectors influence $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$; all other points could be removed without changing the solution.

HINGE LOSS CONNECTION

The soft margin SVM is equivalent to minimizing $\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_i \max(0, 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha))$, where $\ell_{\text{hinge}}(z) = \max(0, 1-z)$ is the hinge loss. This connects SVMs to regularized empirical risk minimization, the framework underlying logistic regression and neural networks.

FEATURE LIFTING MAPS

A map $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D$ transforms data into a higher-dimensional space where a linear classifier induces a non-linear boundary in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The decision function is $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}) + \alpha$. The lifting idea works with any linear classifier, not just SVMs.

PARABOLIC LIFTING THEOREM

The map $\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x}, \|\mathbf{x}\|^2)$ converts hyperspherical separability in $\mathbb{R}^d$ into linear separability in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$, and vice versa. The proof: the sphere equation $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}\|^2 \lessgtr \rho^2$ expands into a linear inequality in $\Phi(\mathbf{x})$.

QUADRIC DECISION BOUNDARIES

The degree-2 lifting map $\Phi_2$ (all squares, cross-products, and linear terms) produces quadric decision boundaries: circles, ellipses, hyperbolas, parabolas, cylinders, two parallel hyperplanes, and hyperplanes as degenerate cases. Lifted dimension is $D_2 = (d^2 + 3d)/2$.

DEGREE-p POLYNOMIAL LIFTING

The degree-$p$ map includes all monomials of total degree $\le p$ (excluding constant), with $D_p = \binom{d+p}{p} - 1$ features. Dimension grows as $O(d^p)$, making direct computation infeasible for large $d$ or $p$. The kernel trick (Chapter 10) resolves this by computing inner products implicitly.

SEPARABILITY THEOREM

Any finite set of distinct labeled points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ can be made linearly separable by lifting to a sufficiently high polynomial degree. However, the required degree may approach $n$ (the number of training points), corresponding to perfect interpolation and severe overfitting. Degree selection must be done by validation.

Exercises

Exercise 9.1 · Soft Margin Primal and Slack Geometry
Deriving Optimal Slack and Verifying the Hinge Loss Equivalence

(a) For fixed $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$, show that the optimal slack for training point $i$ in the soft margin primal is $\zeta_i^* = \max(0,\, 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha))$. Use only the first-order optimality condition with respect to $\zeta_i$.

(b) Substitute the expression from part (a) back into the soft margin objective to obtain the unconstrained formulation $\min_{\mathbf{w},\alpha} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C \sum_i \ell_{\text{hinge}}(y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha))$ where $\ell_{\text{hinge}}(z) = \max(0,1-z)$. Verify that this is equivalent to the primal.

(c) Consider a 1D problem with training points $\{(x_i, y_i)\} = \{(0.5, +1), (1.5, +1), (-0.5, -1), (-1.5, -1)\}$. The symmetry forces $\alpha = 0$. For $w > 0$, compute $\sum_i \zeta_i^*(w)$ as a function of $w$. Find the optimal $w^*(C)$ for $C \in \{0.1, 1, 10\}$.

(d) In a spam classification system, the "training points" are email feature vectors and the labels are spam/not-spam. Explain in plain language what a large slack $\zeta_i$ for a particular email means, and why a small $C$ might be preferable in a setting with many mislabeled training emails.

Exercise 9.2 · The Role of C and Validation
Bias-Variance Analysis of the Regularization Hyperparameter

(a) Prove formally that as $C \to \infty$, the soft margin SVM solution converges (in the linearly separable case) to the hard margin SVM solution. Specifically, show that in the limit, all slack variables must be zero at any optimal solution.

(b) For the same training set (fixed $\mathbf{x}_i, y_i$), show that the optimal value of the objective $\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}^*(C)\|^2 + C\sum_i \zeta_i^*(C)$ is non-decreasing in $C$. Is $\|\mathbf{w}^*(C)\|$ non-decreasing or non-increasing in $C$? Prove your answer.

(c) Consider a dataset where the optimal $C$ found by 5-fold cross-validation is $C^* = 10$. A colleague argues that they should use $C = 10^6$ to get higher training accuracy. Write a quantitative argument (in terms of the bias-variance tradeoff) explaining why this is likely to produce worse test accuracy.

(d) Propose a practical strategy for hyperparameter search when the computational budget allows only 20 evaluations. Should you use a uniform grid, a logarithmic grid, or random search? Justify your answer with reference to the structure of the U-shaped validation error curve.

Exercise 9.3 · Parabolic Lifting and the Sphere Theorem
Circular Boundaries in Medical Image Classification

(a) Let $d = 2$. The parabolic lifting map gives $\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = (x_1, x_2, x_1^2 + x_2^2)^\top$. Suppose the optimal linear classifier in $\Phi$-space has weight vector $\mathbf{w} = (-2c_1, -2c_2, 1)^\top$ and bias $\alpha^* = c_1^2 + c_2^2 - \rho^2$. Write down the decision boundary $\{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{w} \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}) + \alpha^* = 0\}$ and show it is a circle with center $(c_1, c_2)$ and radius $\rho$.

(b) The proof of the Parabolic Lifting Theorem (Section 9.5.3) handles the case $v_{d+1} \neq 0$. What geometric object does the decision boundary in $\mathbb{R}^d$ become when $v_{d+1} = 0$? Verify this claim directly.

(c) In a medical imaging task, cell nuclei from biopsy images are described by two features: mean radius $x_1$ and mean texture $x_2$. Malignant nuclei (class $+1$) tend to have large values of $x_1^2 + x_2^2$ (far from origin in feature space), while benign nuclei (class $-1$) cluster near the origin. Describe the feature lifting you would apply and explain why it should produce a well-separated dataset in the lifted space.

(d) The theorem assumes the boundary is a single hypersphere. What additional feature(s) would you add to handle a dataset separable by two concentric spheres (i.e., points in an annular region form one class)? Derive the decision function and the structure of the new lifting map.

Exercise 9.4 · Quadric Features in Practice
Conic Sections for Non-Linear Classification in Genomics

(a) For $d = 2$, the degree-2 lifting gives a 5-dimensional feature space. Write out the matrix equation $\mathbf{w}^\top \Phi_2(\mathbf{x}) + G = 0$ explicitly, identifying each coefficient with the standard conic section notation $Ax_1^2 + Bx_2^2 + Dx_1 x_2 + Ex_1 + Fx_2 + G = 0$. Under what conditions on $(A, B, D)$ is this conic an ellipse? A hyperbola? A parabola?

(b) Prove that any linear decision boundary in the original space $\mathbb{R}^d$ can also be represented as a quadric decision boundary (i.e., a degree-2 SVM applied to $\Phi_2(\mathbf{x})$ can always recover a linear boundary). This shows that degree-2 features are a strict generalization of linear features.

(c) Compute the dimension $D_2$ of the degree-2 lifted space for $d = 5, 10, 50, 100, 500$. At what value of $d$ does the lifted dimension first exceed $10^6$?

(d) In a genomics application, you have $d = 200$ gene expression features and $n = 500$ labeled samples. Compare the number of parameters in a linear SVM, a degree-2 SVM (with explicit feature map), and a degree-3 SVM. Which model risks overfitting the most? How would you use $C$ to partially mitigate this risk?

Exercise 9.5 · Polynomial Features: Expressiveness vs. Complexity
Degree Selection for Text Classification with Bag-of-Words Features

(a) State and prove (or prove by construction) that for any $n$ distinct points $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with binary labels, there exists a polynomial $q: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree at most $n-1$ such that $\text{sign}(q(\mathbf{x}_i)) = y_i$ for all $i$. Why does this not contradict the fact that high-degree polynomials generalize poorly?

(b) Consider lifting a $d$-dimensional dataset to degree $p = 2$ vs. $p = 4$. For $d = 10$, compute the lifted dimension for each. If the SVM training time scales as $O(D^2)$ in the dimension $D$ of the lifted space (a rough model for QP complexity), estimate the ratio of training times.

(c) In text classification, raw features are word counts — vectors $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{10000}$ (one per word in the vocabulary). Why is it computationally infeasible to use a degree-2 explicit lifting map here? Describe in one sentence how the kernel trick (to be introduced in Chapter 10) resolves this problem without explicitly constructing $\Phi_2(\mathbf{x})$.

(d) A practitioner applies polynomial lifting with $p = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ to the same dataset and observes the following 5-fold cross-validation errors: $0.18, 0.11, 0.09, 0.10, 0.14$. Which degree should they use? Describe the experimental protocol (including how they should tune $C$ jointly with $p$) for a rigorous model selection procedure.
